options: Not changeable
Not readable
Not encrypted
Not stored
Not related
questions.explanation: Immutable means not changeable; the immutable data warehouse takes its name from immutable data.

questions.stem: Why is data in a database described as mutable?
options: Because it can be read by many users at once
Because after inserting it, one also has the option to change it using update or delete commands
Because it is stored on rotating disks
Because it is normalised to 3NF
Because it must be encrypted
questions.explanation: When inserting new data into a database, one also has the option to change it using update or delete commands, which means the data is mutable.

questions.stem: At the technology level, what must every database or data store allow?
options: Only inserts, never updates
Updates and deletes, because mutability is a must-have at technology level
Automatic deletion of records older than one year
Only read access for business users
Storage across national borders
questions.explanation: The mutable feature is a must-have at technology level: any database must allow update or delete. Whether one should do so can be a business requirement but never a technology limitation.

questions.stem: By default, what kind of datastore is a data warehouse?
options: A mutable datastore
An immutable datastore
A virtual datastore
A federated datastore
An in-memory datastore
questions.explanation: By default, a data warehouse is an immutable datastore.

questions.stem: In the CUSTOMER data set example, which attributes are treated as immutable?
options: Address and contact details
Jobs and cars
Name, date of birth, parents and children
Purchase history and preferences
Email and telephone number
questions.explanation: Customer details like name, date of birth, parents and children are immutable: they cannot and should not be changed or deleted.

questions.stem: In the CUSTOMER data set example, why are address, contact details, jobs and cars considered mutable?
options: Because they are never stored in a warehouse
Because a customer can change them, such as moving house or changing contact details
Because they are not part of the metadata
Because they are stored in fact tables
Because they are always encrypted
questions.explanation: Address, contact details, jobs and cars are mutable information, as a customer can change his or her address or contact details over time.

questions.stem: Where should the immutable or mutable behaviour of each data element be captured, and who should manage it?
options: In the BI tool, managed by business users
In metadata, managed by the Data Governance team
In the application code, managed by developers
In the backup policy, managed by the DBA
In the ACL, managed by the security team
questions.explanation: Both the immutable and the mutable behaviour must be captured in metadata and managed by the Data Governance team.

questions.stem: In a data warehouse or data lake, for which tables is immutable behaviour a given?
options: Dimension tables
Staging tables
Fact tables
Lookup tables
Audit tables
questions.explanation: When we come to the data warehouse and data lake, immutable behaviour is a given for fact tables, while dimensions can be mutable based on the type of dimension.

questions.stem: What does the insurance business example illustrate about historical data in a data warehouse?
options: That all historical data must always be stored
That what history to keep depends on the nature of the business, so irrelevant elements such as address changes may not be stored
That insurers must store every address change
That fact tables should be mutable in insurance
That insurers do not need a data warehouse
questions.explanation: An insurer does not care how many times you changed your address but wants history such as health, family and eating habits, so an insurance warehouse might not even store irrelevant data elements.

questions.stem: What is the architectural purpose of any data warehouse or data mart with respect to history?
options: To overwrite transactions with their latest state
To keep historical transactional data residing in fact tables
To delete data older than the retention period
To store only current dimension values
To virtualise transactions from source systems
questions.explanation: The architecture of any data warehouse or data mart is to keep historical transactional data residing in fact tables, whereas dimension data can be mutable depending on the dimension type.
